notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for **Jeremiah 47**, drawn from the sources I could reach.

---

## Jeremiah 47 — Judgment on the Philistines

### v. 1 — Introduction and Historical Setting

"This is the word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet about the Philistines before Pharaoh struck down Gaza."

- **Traditional reading:** The prophecy is dated "before Pharaoh smote Gaza." The Pharaoh is generally identified as **Pharaoh Necho (Neco)**. Calvin identifies him as Pharaoh-Hophra, who on his retreat from the failed relief of Jerusalem plundered Gaza in passing to show his expedition was not entirely in vain. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-47.html#verse-1] Gill notes Jewish tradition placing this in the 8th or 10th year of Zedekiah, but considers it more likely that Pharaoh-Necho struck Gaza either when marching to Carchemish or on his return after killing Josiah. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/47.htm] Ellicott cites Herodotus (ii.159), who records that after the battle at Megiddo, Necho overthrew Kadytis, usually identified with Gaza. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/47.htm]

- **Why the dating matters:** Matthew Henry notes the prophecy was given when the Philistines were "in their full strength and lustre, themselves and their cities in good condition, in no peril from any adversary." When no human probabilities foresaw danger, Jeremiah foretold their ruin. Pharaoh's smiting of Gaza would be merely the "beginning of sorrows" and an earnest of the greater judgment to come. [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/47-1.html]

- **Calvin (Reformed) explains the purpose:** God prophesied against the Philistines to testify His paternal love toward Israel, undertaking their cause and avenging the wrongs done to them. This gave Israel reason for patience, to wait until God fulfilled the prophecy. The smiting of Gaza by Pharaoh was only a prelude; the far greater judgment would come from the Chaldeans. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-47.html#verse-1]

- **Constable (evangelical):** The most probable date is 609 B.C. (Necho's campaign), since Nebuchadnezzar invaded Ashkelon in 604 B.C. and that invasion was still future when Jeremiah gave this oracle. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-47.html]

---

### v. 2 — Waters Rising from the North

"This is what the LORD says: 'See how the waters are rising from the north and becoming an overflowing torrent. They will overflow the land and its fullness, the cities and their inhabitants. The people will cry out, and all who dwell in the land will wail.'"

- **Traditional reading:** The "waters from the north" is a metaphor for the invading Babylonian (Chaldean) army. As Gill notes, the Targum paraphrases it as "people shall come from the north," i.e., from Chaldea, which lay north of Palestine. They would come with great force and rapidity like an overflowing flood. [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/47-1.html] The flood imagery echoes Isaiah 8:7. Ellicott confirms: the "north" indicates the invasion is Nebuchadnezzar's, not Pharaoh-Necho's. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/47.htm]

- **JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown):** The Chaldeans from the north are compared to the overwhelming waters of their own Euphrates. The smiting of Gaza was to be only the prelude of a greater disaster. Nebuzaradan was left by Nebuchadnezzar after taking Jerusalem to subdue the rest of the adjoining cities and country. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/jeremiah-47.html]

- **David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic):** The Babylonians came not only to conquer Judah and Egypt but to rule the entire region. They would overwhelm the Philistines as floodwaters overwhelm a land. This "from the north" pattern appears throughout Jeremiah's prophecies against surrounding nations. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-47/]

- **Calvin:** There is an implied comparison: the Egyptians merely plundered Gaza's wealth (which was "endurable"), but the Chaldeans would come to exercise boundless cruelty like a flood, utterly destroying it. The "fullness" of the land refers to its wealth — corn, trees, animals, all that enriches it. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-47.html#verse-2]

---

### v. 3 — The Terror of the Invading Army

"at the sound of the galloping hooves of stallions, the rumbling of chariots, and the clatter of their wheels. The fathers will not turn back for their sons; their hands will hang limp."

- **Traditional reading:** The vivid soundscape — stamping hooves, rushing chariots, rumbling wheels — describes the sheer terror of the Babylonian advance. **JFB** explains that "fathers shall not look back to their children" means each person will think only of his own safety; even natural affection is crushed by desperate calamity. "Feebleness of hands" means the hands, the principal instruments of action, lose all power; their only hope is in their feet to flee. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/jeremiah-47.html]

- **Calvin:** That fathers would not care for their children is "a proof of extreme sorrow." Even in adversity men do not divest themselves of natural feelings; when a father forgets he is a parent, it shows the greatest grief — as though men, "having changed their nature, were become logs of wood." "Dissolution of hands" means loss of courage; when hands are relaxed and feeble, men become "as it were inanimate." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-47.html#verse-3]

- **Ellicott:** "The selfishness of panic was to reach its highest point, and to crush out the instincts of natural affection. Even fathers would be content to save themselves, regardless of their children's lives." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/47.htm]

- **Gill:** The terror would be so great that parents would flee precipitously, not even thinking of their children or staying to save them, "being so terrified as not to be able to lift up their hands." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/47-3.htm]

---

### v. 4 — The Day of Total Destruction

"For the day has come to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every remaining ally. Indeed, the LORD is about to destroy the Philistines, the remnant from the coasts of Caphtor."

- **Caphtor:** The traditional identification is with **Crete**, the Philistines' original homeland (cf. Amos 9:7; Deuteronomy 2:23). Harrison (cited by Guzik) states: "Caphtor is the Old Testament designation of Crete." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-47/] However, Ellicott notes multiple proposed identifications — Crete, Cyprus, Caria, Cappadocia, and the Nile Delta (where the name would connect with "Coptic"). Genesis 10:14 connects both Philistines and Caphtorim with Mizraim (Egypt). Ellicott adds there is "a touch of scorn" in calling them the mere "remnant of Caphtor." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/47.htm]

- **Tyre and Sidon:** These were Phoenician, not Philistine cities, but they were probably allied with the Philistines against Babylonia. Guzik, citing Harrison: "The obscure clause 'to cut off from Tyre and Sidon' seems to mean that any available Phoenician help would be prevented from reaching Philistia." Cundall adds: "Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician, not Philistine, cities, but they were probably in a desperate alliance with the Philistines against the overwhelming might of Babylonia." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-47/] Ellicott suggests the "helper that remaineth" may refer to foreign mercenaries (especially Philistines) employed by Tyre and Sidon. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/47.htm]

- **Calvin:** Tyre and Sidon are included because they were part of the same coastal region. They were the "defenses, as it were, of the whole country," and their destruction showed that nothing would be safe throughout the whole land. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-47.html#verse-4]

---

### v. 5 — Mourning in Gaza and Ashkelon

"The people of Gaza will shave their heads in mourning; Ashkelon will be silenced. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourself?"

- **Baldness as mourning:** Shaving the head and cutting oneself were pagan signs of extreme grief (cf. Jeremiah 16:6; 48:37; Leviticus 19:28 forbade Israelites from such practices). Clarke: "They have cut off their hair in token of deep sorrow and distress." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-47/] Ellicott adds baldness is also a sign of "extremest desolation" (Isaiah 7:20). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/47.htm]

- **"Remnant of their valley"** — the LXX reads "remnant of the Anakim" instead of "their valley." Ellicott explains: the Hebrew word for "their valley" (עמק, `emeq) resembles the word for the Anakim, the aboriginal giant race that survived in Philistine cities (Joshua 11:21-22; cf. Goliath of Gath in 1 Samuel 17). The RSV adopts this reading. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/47.htm] JFB, however, defends "their valley" as the long strip of low plain occupied by the Philistines along the Mediterranean, west of the Judean mountains. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/jeremiah-47.html]

- **"How long will you gash yourself?"** — Ellicott notes this points to a pagan ritual of supplication, like the priests of Baal in 1 Kings 18:28. The question implies the mourning will be prolonged and futile. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/47.htm] **Ironside** (Plymouth Brethren): "Baldness indicates the absence of both strength and glory. Philistia should be weak and helpless before her foes; her glory a mere memory." [from search results — StudyLight Ironside]

- **Calvin:** The question "How long wilt thou cut thyself?" means there would be no end to their calamities. Even grievously afflicted people do not perpetually mourn, for time alleviates grief. But here, "evils would be heaped on evils," renewing the cause of mourning daily. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-47.html#verse-5]

---

### v. 6 — The Cry to the Sword of the LORD

"'Alas, O sword of the LORD, how long until you rest? Return to your sheath; cease and be still!'"

- **The personification:** This is widely regarded as one of the most striking figures in the chapter. **Clarke** (Methodist/Wesleyan): "This is a most grand prosopopoeia — a dialogue between the sword of the Lord and the prophet. Nothing can be imagined more sublime." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-47/] The "sword of the LORD" is the Babylonian army, acting as God's instrument of judgment (cf. Jeremiah 12:12; Isaiah 34:6).

- **Who is speaking?** Two views:
  1. **The Philistines** are crying out for the slaughter to end. Ellicott: "This is the question and entreaty of the Philistines, 'When will there be an end of war?'" [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/47.htm]
  2. **Jeremiah himself** in compassion. Gill suggests either: "these are either the words of the Philistines, entreating a stop might be put to the ravages of the sword … or rather of the prophet, commiserating their state as a man, though they had been the avowed enemies of his people." [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/47.htm] Henry also sees it as the prophet's own cry: "This expresses the prophet's earnest desire to see an end of the war, looking with compassion, as became a man, even upon the Philistines themselves." [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/47-1.html]

- **The Expositor's Bible:** "The prophet ceases to be the mouthpiece of God, and breaks out into the cry of human anguish. How often since … men have uttered a like appeal to an unanswering and relentless Providence!" The cry "How long" has been wrung from despairing lips across centuries. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/jeremiah/47.htm]

- **Guzik** applies this to believers today: God's word functions like this sword — "it pierces deep and will not be stilled until it finishes its work in believers' hearts." Citing F.B. Meyer: "O sword of the Lord; thou hast wounded us sore! Like a two-edged sword, the Word of God has pierced to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit … And even now it cannot rest." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-47/]

---

### v. 7 — The Sword Cannot Rest

"How can it rest when the LORD has commanded it? He has appointed it against Ashkelon and the shore of its coastland."

- **The answer:** The sword cannot be sheathed because God has given it a divine commission. **Clarke:** "This is the answer of the Sword. I am the officer of God's judgments, and he has given me a commission against Ashkelon, and against the sea shore; all the coast where the Philistines have their territories." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-47/]

- **Gill:** "How can it be quiet … to stop it is impossible, and to request that it might be stopped is in vain … seeing the Lord hath given it a charge" — the sword has a commission from the Lord, and there "hath he appointed it" by an "irreversible decree of his, in righteousness to punish the inhabitants of these places for their sins." [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/jeremiah/47.htm]

- **Historical fulfillment:** Guzik cites Kidner: "A Babylonian prism, now in Istanbul, mentions the presence — presumably with little choice in the matter — of the kings of Tyre and Sidon, of Gaza, and of Ashdod, at the court of Nebuchadnezzar, while a prison list now in Berlin records the rations for the king of Ashkelon, among other noted prisoners (including Jehoiachin of Judah)." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-47/]

- **Calvin** emphasizes the solemnity of God's decree: God "bound his sword, as it were, by solemn protest … this decree could not be revoked, because God will not only command his sword to execute his vengeance, but will also give it a solemn command, and bind it, as it were, by an oath, never to cease from its work until the whole people, and all the cities, and the whole land, should be destroyed together." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-47.html#verse-7]

- **Utley (bible.org / evangelical):** "There is no rest for YHWH's sword because the conquest of Palestine by Babylon is His will … YHWH is in charge of world history! He now uses Babylon, as He previously used Assyria and will use Persia in the future, to accomplish His purposes." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/jeremiah-47.html]

- **The Expositor's Bible** adds a note of hope beyond judgment: "Yet Ashkelon survived to be a stronghold of the Crusaders, and Gaza to be captured by Alexander and even by Napoleon. Jehovah has other instruments besides His devastating sword; the victorious endurance and recuperative vitality of men and nations also come from Him." It quotes Hosea 6:1 — "He hath torn, and He will heal us; He hath smitten, and He will bind us up." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/jeremiah/47.htm]

- **Henry (Anglican/Puritan)** provides a pastoral application: "When the sword is drawn we cannot expect it should be sheathed till it has fulfilled its charge. As the word of God, so his rod and his sword, shall accomplish that for which he sends them." [https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/47-1.html]

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Emphases

| Tradition | Source | Distinctive Emphasis |
|---|---|---|
| **Reformed** | Calvin | God's sovereignty over history; the irrevocable nature of divine decrees; judgment on Philistines as proof of God's paternal love for Israel. |
| **Methodist/Wesleyan** | Clarke | The literary beauty of the passage; "baldness" as a token of deep distress; the "prosopopoeia" as sublime. |
| **Baptist (Particular)** | Gill | Detailed historical & linguistic analysis; the "irreversible decree" of God; careful consideration of alternative interpretations. |
| **Anglican/Puritan** | Matthew Henry | Pastoral warmth; the prophet's compassion even for enemies; the sword must fulfill its charge; application to the blessings of peace. |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** | David Guzik (Enduring Word) | Application of the "sword" to God's Word piercing believers' hearts; historical confirmation from archaeology; accessible, devotional tone. |
| **Plymouth Brethren** | Ironside | Baldness as loss of strength and glory; God using even pagan armies while not authorizing their cruelties; God as "Governor of the world." |

---

**On differences between traditions:** No major doctrinal disputes emerged among Protestant traditions on this chapter. All agree on the essential points: the Babylonians are the "waters from the north," Caphtor = Crete, and the "sword of the LORD" personifies divine judgment through Babylon. Minor differences concern the identification of which Pharaoh (Necho vs. Hophra), the dating (609 vs. 601 B.C.), and whether v. 6 is spoken by the Philistines or by Jeremiah.

**Catholic, Orthodox, and modern scholarship sources** (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) could not be reached within the available search and fetch limits for this chapter.
